title: How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers
author: Anastasia Lennon
content:
On a hot July day in 2022, then-President Joe Biden gave a speech from the
ruins of a coal-fired power plant on the southern coast of Massachusetts.

Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock
would soon launch components for wind power out to sea.

He praised an Italian company’s plans to build a new factory there, set to
create 250 jobs and supply American-made undersea power cables to what was
then a line of offshore wind projects waiting to be built along the coast.

Four years later, weeds and tall grass have reclaimed the dirt lot on which
Biden spoke.

The company never came.

![President Joe Biden stands at a lectern on a small stage in a muddy field.
In the distant background is a body of water and a cityscape. In the
foreground is a crowd of people.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Biden-original-PD-
edit_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000-1.jpg?w=752)Ben Berke/Ocean State Media
![The same field as the previous picture, photographed from a near-identical
vantage point. Now, the stage is gone, the field is overgrown with weeds and
there are no people.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/DSC08210-2_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Eleonora
Bianchi/The New Bedford Light

Then-President Joe Biden gave a speech at Brayton Point in Somerset,
Massachusetts, in 2022. Four years later, the promised factory has been
canceled.

![An architectural rendering showing an aerial view of a small island with a
large, industrial-looking building on it and a ship just
offshore.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Prysmian-
rendering-PDcrop_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Prysmian ![A
photograph of the same aerial view. The island is mostly empty, with a large
patch of dirt, some greenery and a few small
buildings.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260916-Kenna-
OffshoreWinds-57_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Caleb Kenna for
ProPublica

An architectural rendering of plans for an offshore wind cable factory on
Brayton Point, compared with a 2026 photograph of the same area.

A 20-minute drive east, in New Bedford, hundreds of workers who helped
assemble wind turbine parts from Canada and Europe over the last three years
have given way to seagulls and geese. The birds shuffle along the now-empty
pier the state of Massachusetts spent $140 million to build for offshore wind
development.

In nearby Providence, Rhode Island, a newly built factory that manufactured
offshore wind turbine foundation platforms has emptied out.

![A pier on the ocean with numerous industrial buildings and
cranes.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_7869-PDedit_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Ben
Berke/Ocean State Media ![A nearly identical view of the same pier as the
previous photograph. Now, all the buildings and cranes are
gone.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/DSC07825_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Eleonora
Bianchi/The New Bedford Light

Union members worked for three years assembling turbines on New Bedford’s
waterfront. The wind developer that planned to use the port facility next has
instead delayed its project indefinitely.

Amid the Trump administration’s multifront war against offshore wind, the cost
on the ground in New England, the launchpad of the country’s offshore wind
industry, can be seen in empty warehouses, silent marine terminals and ledgers
recording hundreds of millions of dollars of state investment that may not be
recouped.

ProPublica partnered with Ocean State Media, The Connecticut Mirror and the
New Bedford Light to document the consequences of the administration’s
efforts.

![People wearing blue hard hats and bright neon jackets lift machinery parts
in a warehouse filled with heavy equipment.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/h_15871527-MOBILE_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)James
Estrin/The New York Times/Redux ![A nearly identical view of the same
warehouse, now completely empty.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/DSC09007-MOBILE_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Eleonora
Bianchi/The New Bedford Light

A factory that made turbine components on Providence’s waterfront is now
sitting empty.

Many offshore wind projects faced a precarious future before President Donald
Trump retook office. Rising construction costs driven by inflation and supply
chain shortages forced some developers to back out of contracts to build wind
farms and supply electricity to states. Various groups have also fought
construction of projects saying they disrupt marine ecosystems and mar coastal
views.

But last year, the administration [temporarily forced five projects to stop
construction](https://newbedfordlight.org/offshore-wind-tracker-whats-
happening-to-massachusetts-projects/), further clouding the horizon. Courts
allowed the developers to proceed, but that has not eliminated the threat.
Last month, the U.S. Department of the Interior asked a court for permission
to reconsider a key permit for one of those five projects, Revolution Wind,
which is already up and running and can power more than 350,000 New England
homes at maximum capacity.

The administration also has frozen future development on all offshore wind
farms, including a cluster of projects that haven’t been built but proposed to
power up to 1.7 million New England homes. It has blocked or is seeking review
of the permits that would allow these to be built. Meanwhile, [the
administration is paying other wind developers
](https://apnews.com/article/trump-offshore-wind-energy-climate-interior-
invenergy-2809c57fa04b59a21927631b91b4b69f)billions of dollars to sell back
their leases and walk away.

At a press conference Monday, Trump said he supports a bipartisan bill that
would accelerate U.S. energy development. When [a reporter pointed
out](https://x.com/Acyn/status/2119918741341528345?s=20) that the bill
includes wind energy, Trump said he would not approve “wind turbines ’cause
wind turbines are a major loser.”

The upheaval has had ripple effects. The cable company Biden touted decided
not to build its factory, citing “long-term trends in the U.S. market.”

Port cities like New Bedford, Massachusetts, and New London, Connecticut, are
left trying to hold onto the economic gains they have made building wind
farms.

### Read More About On-the-Ground Impacts From Our Partners

**The Connecticut Mirror:**[Offshore wind offered a 'limitless' future for
Connecticut. Trump scuttled the
plan.](https://ctmirror.org/2026/11/13/offshore-wind-new-london-connecticut-
trump/)

**The New Bedford Light:**[Fishermen’s offshore wind work drying
up](https://newbedfordlight.org/fishermens-offshore-wind-work-drying-up/)

**Ocean State Media:**[Offshore wind saved a struggling New Bedford union. Now
its future is uncertain.](https://www.oceanstatemedia.org/climate-
environment/2026-11-13/offshore-wind-saved-a-struggling-new-bedford-union-now-
its-future-is-uncertain)

As recently as last winter, New Bedford, a historic whaling and textile
manufacturing center, had hotels, offices and piers buzzing with offshore wind
workers. Local businesses from caterers to cleaners to fuel suppliers landed
new contracts servicing the wind industry.

In New London — another port once central to the whaling industry — officials
worked with one of the world’s largest wind developers to pump more than $300
million of public and private funds into a state-owned pier. Despite
significant cost overruns and some early construction challenges, the effort
transformed the pier into a staging area for the wind industry.

![An aerial view of a pier, where heavy machinery is arranged. In the
background is the ocean and a cityscape.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/PROPUBLICA-WIND-0918-SG-05.jpg?w=752)Wind turbine
components are stored at the State Pier in New London, waiting to be loaded
onto installation vessels en route to Danish wind developer Ørsted’s offshore
wind farms. The last of three consecutive projects is expected to be completed
next year, but no others are fully permitted.  Sarah Gordon/The Connecticut
Mirror

Over the last four years, the pier has been a hive of activity. Hundreds of
workers were employed loading and offloading turbine parts — with blades the
length of a football field — from specially designed ships, some with names
drawn from Greek mythology. Local companies also found work supporting the
industry, including one that offered water rescue training for people working
on construction sites offshore.

“I think [the future just looked
limitless,](https://ctmirror.org/2026/11/13/offshore-wind-new-london-
connecticut-trump/)” said New London Mayor Michael Passero.

Before wind, Passero said that officials tried for years to attract different
industries to the pier, which is overshadowed by larger port facilities in New
York and Boston. It was often used to import and store large piles of road
salt.

![A man in a suit jacket stands in front of a large body of water with a pier
in the distant background.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/NL-WIND-
PASSERO-0925-SG-01-MOBILE_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)New London
Mayor Michael Passero in front of the New London State Pier. Danish wind
developer Ørsted is currently using the pier as a staging area for its
offshore wind projects, but no tenants are lined up once that work is
completed. Sarah Gordon/The Connecticut Mirror

The most recent wind project based at the pier is scheduled to finish work
next year. Port officials have yet to find a tenant to occupy the space.  

“They’ll be back to the old days of trying to lure cargo here,” Passero said.

Amid Trump’s war on wind, a frontline of union and nonunion workers watches
opportunity disappear. One project alone, Vineyard Wind, directly employed a
total of more than 3,700 full- and part-time workers — most of them from
Massachusetts — over eight years of development and construction, according to
the developer.

![A woman wearing a hard hat stands in front of cranes, wind turbine
components and trailers.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/DSC02369-MOBILE_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)
![A nearly identical view of the same area. All the people, machinery and
buildings are gone, and instead there are geese and
seagulls.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/DSC07928-3-MOBILE_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)

Sónia Brito, a New Bedford native, worked at the New Bedford terminal for at
least two years. She is now taking classes through the Millwrights’ union in
New Jersey, in hopes of staying in the wind industry. Geese and seagulls have
reclaimed the space previously occupied by workers and turbine parts. Eleonora
Bianchi/The New Bedford Light

During peak construction activity, as many as 300 union members worked onshore
in southeastern Massachusetts for the project, the first large offshore wind
farm fully permitted by the federal government. The wind farm was completed
this year.

Longshoreman Onix Vazquez, 34, worked full-time tying up barges and moving
turbine components on and off New Bedford’s wind pier. He grew up a few blocks
away and said he had struggled to find lucrative work until Vineyard Wind
began hiring from his union.

![A man wearing sunglasses stands in front of a body of water and
boats.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/DSC09529-1.jpg?w=1149)Onix Vazquez, a New Bedford
longshoreman, said his hourly wage nearly doubled when he started working in
the wind industry. Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light

Vazquez’s hourly wage of $50 was nearly double what he previously earned
unloading occasional shipments of tangerines and juice concentrate. It allowed
him and other members of his [historically Black union
](https://www.oceanstatemedia.org/climate-environment/2026-11-13/offshore-
wind-saved-a-struggling-new-bedford-union-now-its-future-is-uncertain)to make
down payments on houses, pay off medical bills and for the first time take
their families on out-of-state vacations.

“Most of us have to get other jobs for now or collect unemployment,” said
Kevin Rose, president of New Bedford’s longshoremen union, which put about two
dozen members to work on the project.

The union had been planning to rebuild its nearby meeting hall, which was
demolished a decade earlier when work grew scarce. But the next developer to
lease New Bedford’s wind pier has delayed its project indefinitely. The union
members have put the plans for their new hall on hold.  

Vazquez said he now works a seasonal job in the cranberry industry for much
lower pay.

“They don’t see that it affects us, the ones that work the projects,” he said.

![A black and white photograph of three men sitting at a table. Behind them is
an American flag and a banner that says, “International Longshoremen’s Assoc.
Local - 1413-1465.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/JDT-N-85.06B_0009-Longshoremen-New-Bedford-
MOBILE_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Spinner Publications ![An empty
lot where a building used to stand. Grass grows through the
pavement.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/DSC07501-MOBILE_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Eleonora
Bianchi/The New Bedford Light

The longshoremen’s union hall in New Bedford in 1985 and the empty lot that
now stands in its place. New Bedford’s longshoremen planned to rebuild it
after members found work in the offshore wind industry. They’ve since put
those plans on hold.

In response to questions about the impact of the administration’s actions on
American offshore wind workers, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of the
Interior repeated criticisms of offshore wind as an expensive and unreliable
source of energy.

“The reality is that the Biden administration lured companies into these
projects with the promise of millions of taxpayer dollars in subsidies to make
these offshore wind projects viable,” the spokesperson said in an email.

The view is more nuanced [on the
ground.](https://newbedfordlight.org/fishermens-offshore-wind-work-drying-up/)
New Bedford’s fishing industry is generally critical of wind farm development
because fishermen worry about disruption to fishing grounds.

But fishing catch limits keep boats tied to docks for much of the year. Work
for wind farms gets them out to sea and helps pay the bills.

Over the past few years of construction, Vineyard Wind paid about $11 million
to 55 fishing vessels from New England and an estimated 60 to 70 fishermen,
according to the developer. (The figure also covers fuel.) The fishermen look
out for protected species, guard exposed underwater cable as it’s being laid
and log information for the developer.

Some fishermen say they will work in offshore wind for as long as they can.

“The scallop boats need the extra revenue,” said Patrick Walsh, 37, a fifth-
generation fisherman who plans to rejoin his father’s fishing business when
wind work wraps up. “The worst thing for a boat is to sit. Those boats are
made to work.”

Wind farm work made it possible for him to buy his first house, he said.

“Fishing would pay bills, and wind was going in the bank.”

![A man stands on a boat, looking at the camera as he reaches up to hold a
rope. His T-shirt says “Walsh” and has an icon of an
anchor.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/DSC01395-2_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Patrick
Walsh is a fifth-generation fisherman who has pivoted to working on wind
projects for the past few years. Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light
